newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Tennis-Belgian unknown rules roost on centre court.
newsitem.headline: Tennis-Belgian unknown rules roost on centre court.

text.p: Belgium's Dominique van Roost stepped on to centre court at Melbourne Park on Saturday as a virtual unknown, her nerves playing havoc before her first appearance on a grand slam stadium court.
She returned to the locker room 2-1/2 half hours later with a standing ovation ringing in her ears, but said fame was far from her mind.
"I am normal, I am human, I am a human being, I am like you, so I don't feel like I should be a star," she said.
Van Roost's come-from-nowhere 1-6 6-4 8-6 win over Spain's world number three Arantxa Sanchez Vicario in the third round was the biggest women's upset yet in this year's Australian Open.
For sheer improbability it even rivalled defending champion Boris Becker's first-round defeat by Spanish clay court specialist Carlos Moya.
"I don't realise at the moment what I just did. Probably in a few hours," said Van Roost.
After being totally overpowered in the first set, the slender, photogenic Belgian found a source of strength to turn the match around and beat a woman ranked 40 places above her.
A natural baseliner, she forced herself to the net knowing that her only chance against the Spaniard was to be aggressive, to hit the ball as hard as her slight frame allowed.

The transformation caught Sanchez Vicario off her guard in the second set but the third became a scrap. The Spaniard built a 5-2 lead only to lose the next four games as Van Roost threw all her strength into every stroke she played.

Sanchez Vicario broke the Belgian's service to even the score only to have her service broken the following game. After a couple of minutes of massage of her serving arm -- "I was holding my racquet too tight," she said -- Van Roost served out to win the match in two hours and 14 minutes.
Winner of both the French and U.S. Opens, the Spaniard has infamously lost five of the last eight grand slam finals, but this was her worst grand slam performance in five years.
"She has nothing to lose," Sanchez Vicario said of her opponent.
For Van Roost, the win brought instant celebrity, at least at Melbourne Park, where record crowds over the past week have been quick to latch on to the outsiders.
In her small village back home in the French-speaking part of Belgium, Van Roost can walk the streets without people paying any attention. Autograph hunters have never been a problem.
